issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: CngProperty constructor with ReadOnlySpan<byte> overload
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-security, @vcsjones See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Background and motivation There is an internal constructor on `CngProperty` that accepts the `value` as a `ReadOnlySpan`. https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/be20c44826bc55d201c406f4ac007d24ed7a9137/src/libraries/System.Security.Cryptography/src/System/Security/Cryptography/CngProperty.cs#L30 I propose making this public so that callers that have data as a `ReadOnlySpan` don't need to convert it to a `byte[]` first, and then get copied, again, since it keeps a defensive copy. ### API Proposal ```diff namespace System.Security.Cryptography { public partial struct CngProperty { - internal CngProperty(string name, ReadOnlySpan value, CngPropertyOptions options); + public CngProperty(string name, ReadOnlySpan value, CngPropertyOptions options); } } ``` ### API Usage ```csharp ReadOnlySpan value = "I need a nap"u8; CngProperty test = new( "CustomLabel", value, CngPropertyOptions. CustomProperty); ``` ### Alternative Designs _No response_ ### Risks _No response_
Author: vcsjones
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-System.Security`
Milestone: -

I can take a look at it. 
You are welcome to assign me :smile:

review_comments:
@bartonjs alluded to an implementation change that he thought we should consider. 

>There may be some interesting edge cases around null vs empty (and therefore the default ReadOnlySpan vs a zero-width slice) which probably warrant testing (or proving that null and empty are the same to CNG)

Basically change this line:

```C#
_value = value.ToArray();
```

To:

```C#
_value = value == default(ReadOnlySpan<byte>) ? null : value.ToArray();
```

We have, in a few places, decided that a span whose `ref` is `null` should be treated as null.

I do not think that is valuable to do here. In fact there are some cases where `null` results in throwing.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/33ee13071c4a41dec673fe4ef4333ea37f12d183/src/libraries/System.Security.Cryptography.Cng/tests/PropertyTests.cs#L88-L93

People would probably be confused why passing `ReadOnlySpan<byte>.Empty` would result in a CryptographicException. I suppose if someone _really_ wants to pass `null`, then they need to use the `byte[]?` overload. But trying to do "where does this span point to" seems like a pit of failure to me.

So I don't think we should do anything - but I wanted to address Jeremy's comment, and, ensure he concurs.

What I care about is that there's a test that says a CngProperty built on `(byte[])null` is the same as one built on `(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)(byte[])null`, and similarly for `Array.Empty<byte[]>()`.  If that equivalence is met, I don't particularly care what this line of code looks like :smile:.

If a CngProperty based on `null` is basically useless (CNG will never return one, and CNG will never accept one... it can only be used within application code for some random purpose) then my position probably changes to "the null span and the empty span should be the same".  But I want to start with the tests.  Particularly if null and empty are both valid inputs to CNG but mean different things (e.g. if null means "erase this property")

I still don't see tests around this behavior.

There should be a test showing that setting a property to `(byte[])null` (via the byte[] ctor) and `default(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` (via the new ctor) do the same thing.

There should also be a test (same one? different one? surprise me) showing that `Array.Empty<byte>()` (old ctor) and `Array.Empty<byte>().AsSpan()` (new ctor) do the same thing.  They might even do the same thing as `null`.

What sort of things are the same?

* Does HasProperty give the same answer for the same value in both the old and new ctor when assigning a property that the key doesn't already have?
* Does HasProperty give the same answer for the same value in both the old and new ctor when overwriting an existing (non-empty) value?
* Does GetProperty give identical answers for the same value in both the old and new ctor?
* Anything else that feels relevant, though their might not actually be "anything else" since there's not a lot of API surface here.
